n: The main part of the letter contains Paul's guidance on specific problems and questions in the Corinthian church.

Paul now answers the questions the Corinthians asked him in a letter, starting with the topic of marriage (see {{1 Corinthians 7:25|1 Corinthians 7:25}}; {{1 Corinthians 8:1|8:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:1|12:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 16:1|16:1}}).

Paul addresses the Corinthians' question about eating food offered to idols. In the Greco-Roman world, temples and shrines dedicated to pagan gods were common. Worshipers often offered animal sacrifices, and pagan priests sold the extra meat in the market. Christians wondered if they could eat this meat. 

Was meat from a sacrifice to a pagan god impure? Paul does not mention the Jewish Christian leaders' prohibition in {{Acts 15:20|Acts 15:20}}, {{Acts 15:29|29}}. Instead, he stresses that actions should be guided by love and consideration for others. After introducing the topic ({{1 Corinthians 8:1-13|1 Corinthians 8:1–13}}), he shares examples of giving up one's rights for others' sake ({{1 Corinthians 9:1-27|9:1–27}}) and offers advice on three specific situations believers faced.

Paul made it very clear that false gods aren’t real. They aren’t true gods. Food sacrificed to them doesn’t mean anything. Believers are free to eat that food.

But there are two reasons they should be careful. Firstly, when people make sacrifices to false gods they actually honour evil spiritual beings. Believers must refuse anything that joins them to evil.

Secondly, believers must be careful not to confuse people about what is right or wrong. Paul described this like making people trip and fall. People may think that a certain food is wrong to eat. If they see a believer eat that food, they think the believer is doing something evil. This may lead people to doubt the truth about God and to not believe in him.

Believers have the right to eat and drink anything that they thank God for. But there is something more important than using that right. It’s helping people believe in Jesus and follow him. Believers bring glory to God when they do things for the good of others.

Paul concludes the discussion started in {{1 Corinthians 8:1|8:1}} with guidance on when Christians may eat meat offered to an idol and when they should not (see study note on 1 Corinthians 8:1–11:1). His guidance emphasizes the principle of giving up one's rights out of love (see also {{1 Corinthians 8:13-9:23|8:13–9:23}}).

*the traditions, just as I passed them on to you*: This phrase usually means an important tradition of Christian teaching shared by word of mouth (see also {{1 Corinthians 11:23|11:23}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:1-3|15:1–3}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:15|2 Thessalonians 2:15}}).

God is worshipped in different ways in different places and at different times. These ways are often based on what is common and proper where people live.

In Paul’s time in the areas around the Mediterranean Sea, hair was very important. It was considered proper for women to wear their hair long and to cover their heads. That wasn’t considered proper for men.

Corinthian believers who were men wore their hair in a certain way. Corinthian believers who were women did something else with their hair. But all of them prayed, prophesied and worshipped God. They were all under God’s authority.

*the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God*: The word *head *serves as a metaphor for either *source* or *authority*. The immediate context and Paul's overall teaching suggest that *head* means *authority* in this context (see {{Genesis 3:16|Genesis 3:16}}; {{Ephesians 5:21-23|Ephesians 5:21–23}}; {{Colossians 3:18|Colossians 3:18}}; {{1 Peter 3:1|1 Peter 3:1}}).

Paul discusses a woman's use of a head covering. He argues that women who pray or prophesy in public should wear a veil. This is to dress modestly and appropriately during worship (compare {{1 Timothy 2:9|1 Timothy 2:9}}; {{1 Peter 3:3|1 Peter 3:3}}). Some in Corinth were not wearing head coverings, citing freedom in Christ. Paul supports the custom based on social traditions, the Genesis creation story, and the presence of angels.

- In this passage, *head* is used both literally and figuratively. A man who covers his physical head while praying dishonors his spiritual head, Christ. A woman who prays or prophesies without covering her physical head dishonors her spiritual head, her husband. 

- The spiritual gift of prophesying is the God-given ability to speak a specific message from God, not just to predict the future (see {{1 Corinthians 12:10|12:10}}; {{1 Corinthians 14:1-5|14:1–5}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:20|1 Thessalonians 5:20}}). 

- *every woman who prays or prophesies*: Women were allowed to pray and prophesy publicly in the church (see {{Acts 21:9|Acts 21:9}}).
*he is the image and glory of God*: See {{Genesis 1:26-27|Genesis 1:26–27}}.

- *because of the angels*: Angels are guardians of the world, ensuring everything follows God's plan (see {{Genesis 19:1-21|Genesis 19:1–21}}; {{Genesis 22:11-12|22:11–12}}; {{Exodus 23:20|Exodus 23:20}}; {{Numbers 22:22-23|Numbers 22:22–23}}; {{Psalm 34:7|Psalms 34:7}}; {{Psalm 91:11|91:11}}; {{Psalm 103:20-21|103:20–21}}; {{Hebrews 1:7|Hebrews 1:7}}, {{Hebrews 1:14|14}}). Believers should act appropriately in front of others and God's observing angels (compare {{1 Timothy 5:21|1 Timothy 5:21}}). 

- *ought to have a sign of authority on her head*: should wear a covering on her head to show she is under authority.
*But everything comes from God* (compare {{1 Corinthians 8:6|8:6}}): Both men and women must ultimately submit to God, who is the head of all.
*Judge for yourselves…Is it proper?*: This rhetorical question expects the answer "no."
*Doesn't nature itself teach you?*: In Paul's culture, men did not wear long hair.

- Paul argues that social rules about hair length show basic differences between men and women. 

- *For long hair is given to her as a covering*: Paul suggests that women's long hair, which covers their heads, indicates that God wants women to have some form of "covering."

- *If anyone is inclined to dispute this*: Some members of the diverse Corinthian church disagreed with Paul. 

- Paul’s final point is that wearing a head covering was a long-standing church custom. Most modern interpreters believe this custom was based on culture.
*your gatherings*: Early Christians met in someone's home at least once a week, usually on the Lord's Day (see {{1 Corinthians 16:2|16:2}}).

The way that the Corinthian believers shared the Lord’s Supper caused harm to the church. It didn’t show how Jesus’ followers were brought together as one.

The Corinthian church had separated into different groups. Rich people and poor people were treated differently. Some had a feast during the Lord’s Supper and even got drunk. Others were left with nothing to eat.

As a result of this, judgement had come upon the church. Some believers had become sick and others had died.

Paul explained that the Lord’s Supper is about remembering and announcing Jesus’ death. Jesus gave his body as a sacrifice to establish a new covenant with God’s people.

Believers must honour Jesus’ body that was buried and was raised from the dead. Believers must also honour the other believers in the body of Christ. In this way they also honour Jesus. Their worship practices should help them take care of one another as God’s family.
Paul discusses issues with how the Corinthians interact with each other and with the Lord during the Lord's Supper.

The divisions might refer to those mentioned in {{1 Corinthians 1:10-12|1:10–12}} (compare {{Titus 3:10|Titus 3:10}}), or more likely, they result from social discrimination during shared meals (see {{1 Corinthians 11:21-22|1 Corinthians 11:21–22}}, {{1 Corinthians 11:33|33}}; {{Acts 6:1|Acts 6:1}}).

This ironic expression criticizes the Corinthian Christians for claiming superiority based on their differences. Alternatively, Paul might suggest that while their divisiveness is wrong, it will reveal who among them is truly faithful.
Some people cared more about eating their own dinner than about the Lord's Supper.

- *For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you*: This is one of the few clear references in Paul's letters to traditions passed down from Christ (see also {{1 Corinthians 7:10|7:10}}; {{1 Corinthians 9:14|9:14}}; compare {{1 Thessalonians 4:15-17|1 Thessalonians 4:15–17}}). 

- *On the night he was betrayed*: See {{Mark 14:43-46|Mark 14:43–46}}.

- Jews and early Christians traditionally thanked God for their food before eating (see study note on Mark 14:22–25). 

- *This is My body*: Compare {{John 6:32-35|John 6:32–35}}, {{John 6:48-58|48–58}}.

- After supper may suggest that the main meal separated the breaking of the bread from the drinking of the cup (see {{Luke 22:20|Luke 22:20}}). 

- The new covenant is God's promise to forgive sins because of Jesus' sacrificial death (compare {{Jeremiah 31:31-34|Jeremiah 31:31–34}}; {{Jeremiah 32:40|32:40}}; {{Luke 22:20|Luke 22:20}}; {{Hebrews 7:22|Hebrews 7:22}}; {{Hebrews 8:8-10|8:8–10}}; {{Hebrews 9:15|9:15}}; {{Hebrews 10:12-18|10:12–18}}; {{Hebrews 12:24|12:24}}; {{Hebrews 13:20|13:20}}). The blood of a sacrifice confirmed an agreement or covenant (see {{Exodus 24:8|Exodus 24:8}}; {{Zechariah 9:11|Zechariah 9:11}}; {{Hebrews 9:12|Hebrews 9:12}}; {{Hebrews 13:20|13:20}}; compare {{Romans 3:25|Romans 3:25}}; {{Romans 5:9|5:9}}).

When Christians take the Lord’s Supper, they share the importance of the Lord’s death with others until he returns (see {{1 Corinthians 1:7-8|1:7–8}}; compare {{1 Thessalonians 1:9-10|1 Thessalonian 1:9–10}}; {{1 Thessalonians 3:12|3:12}}; {{1 Thessalonians 4:13-18|4:13–18}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:23|5:23}}).

Taking the Lord’s Supper without understanding its importance or with unconfessed sin is unworthy (see {{1 Corinthians 11:28-31|11:28–31}}). It is like sinning against the body and blood of the Lord; it treats his sacrificial death as unimportant (compare {{Hebrews 10:29|Hebrews 10:29}}).
Before taking the Lord's Supper, Christians should confess their sins and think about what the bread and cup mean ({{1 Corinthians 11:26|11:26}}).

- In light of {{1 Corinthians 11:27|11:27}}, the body of Christ likely refers to the death of Christ, not the church, though some interpret it that way. 

- Those who eat the bread or drink the cup in an unworthy manner bring God's judgment upon themselves. This judgment may result in infirmities, sickness, or even death (see {{Acts 5:5|Acts 5:5}}, {{Acts 5:10|10}}).
Judging yourself, which means admitting your sins and repenting, prevents God's judgment.

When God judges and disciplines his people (see {{Deuteronomy 8:5|Deuteronomy 8:5}}; {{Hebrews 12:5-11|Hebrews 12:5–11}}), it is for their ultimate benefit. This ensures they are not condemned with the world (see {{Ephesians 2:1-3|Ephesians 2:1–3}}).
*when I come*: Paul was planning to visit soon ({{1 Corinthians 4:19|4:19}}; {{1 Corinthians 16:5-7|16:5–7}}).
Paul introduces the topic and highlights how the Holy Spirit actively works in believers.

The Holy Spirit helps people recognise that Jesus is Lord and King. Once someone believes in Jesus, the Holy Spirit lives inside them. The Spirit knows them and helps them to live for Jesus and serve him.

The Holy Spirit also gives gifts to believers. The gifts of the Spirit help believers serve one another. The Spirit decides which gift to give to each person. One gift isn’t better than another. Each gift is special and important. They all come from the Holy Spirit. They are all to be used to strengthen the faith of Jesus’ followers.

The church in Corinth focused too much on the gift of speaking in tongues (see {{1 Corinthians 14:1-25|14:1–25}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:27|27}}; compare the lists in {{1 Corinthians 12:8-10|12:8–10}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:28|28}}, where Paul lists tongues last). Paul offers advice to correct their understanding of the value and use of spiritual gifts.
*pagans*: Non-Jewish people who do not follow a major religion.

Paul provides two ways to recognize the Spirit's presence in worship:

- Those who curse Jesus show they reject him and his message, so they cannot speak by the Spirit of God. 

- Believers show the Holy Spirit's presence in their lives by sincerely confessing that Jesus is Lord. This may be the earliest Christian creed (see {{Romans 10:9|Romans 10:9}}, {{Romans 10:13|13}}; {{2 Corinthians 4:5|2 Corinthians 4:5}}; {{Philippians 2:11|Philippians 2:11}}; {{1 John 4:2-3|1 John 4:2–3}}).

Believers are united in the Lord and his Spirit, but God gives different spiritual gifts to each person. These gifts help them serve the same Lord in various ways (see also {{1 Corinthians 7:7|7:7}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:7-11|12:7–11}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:28-31|28–31}}; {{Romans 12:6-8|Romans 12:6–8}}; {{Ephesians 4:11|Ephesians 4:11}}).

All the work believers do for God is actually God working through them (see {{1 Corinthians 15:10|15:10}}; {{2 Corinthians 4:7|2 Corinthians 4:7}}; {{Galatians 2:8|Galatians 2:8}}; {{Philippians 2:13|Philippians 2:13}}; compare {{Galatians 2:20|Galatians 2:20}}).
Spiritual gifts are not for the benefit of the person who receives them. They are meant to help others (see {{1 Peter 4:10-11|1 Peter 4:10–11}}).

- God's Spirit provides supernatural wisdom or knowledge to some believers. 

- *to another the message of knowledge*: see {{1 Corinthians 1:5|1:5}}; {{1 Corinthians 8:1|8:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 13:2|13:2}}, {{1 Corinthians 13:8|8}}.
This list of nine spiritual gifts is an example, not a complete list (see also {{1 Corinthians 12:28-30|12:28–30}}; {{Romans 12:6-8|Romans 12:6–8}}; {{Ephesians 4:11|Ephesians 4:11}}).

The spiritual gift of great faith is different from the faith needed for salvation. It is an exceptional ability to trust God for specific needs (see {{1 Corinthians 13:2|13:2}}; {{Matthew 17:19-20|Matthew 17:19–20}}; compare {{Acts 6:5|Acts 6:5}}; {{Acts 11:24|11:24}}).

- Prophesying means delivering a special message from God, not just predicting the future (see {{1 Corinthians 11:4-5|11:4–5}}; {{1 Corinthians 13:2|13:2}}, {{1 Corinthians 13:8|8}}; {{1 Corinthians 14:1-25|14:1–25}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:29-33|29–33}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:20|1 Thessalonians 5:20}}; compare {{Acts 13:1-2|Acts 13:1–2}}; {{Acts 21:4|21:4}}, {{Acts 21:10-11|10–11}}). 

- The gift to discern if a message is from God's Spirit or another spirit is essential for any Christian community open to God's word (see {{1 Corinthians 14:29|1 Corinthians 14:29}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:19-21|1 Thessalonians 5:19–21}}; compare {{Acts 16:16-18|Acts 16:16–18}}; {{1 John 4:1-3|1 John 4:1–3}}). 

- For Paul, speaking in unknown languages means using a spiritual language that needs the gift of interpretation to be understood. By ranking this gift lower (both here and in {{1 Corinthians 12:28|1 Corinthians 12:28}}), Paul indicates that the gift of tongues is less important, as the Corinthian church had become overly fascinated with it (compare {{1 Corinthians 13:1|13:1}}, {{1 Corinthians 13:8|8}}; {{1 Corinthians 14:1-25|14:1–25}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:27|27}}). 

- The ability to interpret is not about translating with natural skill, but about spiritually understanding the Spirit's message through the gift of tongues (see {{1 Corinthians 14:5|14:5}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:13|13}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:26-28|26–28}}).

*the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines*: See {{1 Corinthians 12:4|12:4}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:6|6}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:18|18}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:28|28}}. Paul affirms both God's choice in giving spiritual gifts and the human duty to "earnestly desire the most helpful gifts" ({{1 Corinthians 12:31|12:31}}).

Paul described several ways that the church is like a body. The church is made up of many kinds of people. They come from different places and have different ways of thinking and doing things. They have different gifts from the Spirit. They work and serve in different ways.

In this way believers are like the different parts of a human body. Also like the parts of a human body, believers work together as one. They work together to obey Jesus and to tell others about him.

Paul also said that the church was in fact the body of Christ. Jesus is like the head that guides and directs the body (Ephesians 5:23). Jesus is now in heaven ruling with the Father.

The church continues to do his work on earth through the power of the Holy Spirit. In this way the church is the part of Jesus that other people see. This is how the church is like Jesus’ body on earth until he returns.

The church is like a body (see {{1 Corinthians 12:27|12:27}}) made up of many different parts. Each part has its own role, as determined by God (see {{1 Corinthians 12:11|12:11}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:18|18}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:28|28}}; {{Romans 12:4-5|Romans 12:4–5}}).

- Ethnic and social differences do not matter in the church (see {{Galatians 3:28|Galatians 3:28}}; {{Colossians 3:11|Colossians 3:11}}). 

- *For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body*: Water baptism represents a spiritual baptism. In this, the Holy Spirit unites the believer with Christ and the church.

These verses shift from the image of a physical body to the image of the church as a spiritual body. Every part of the body is important and essential for it to work well. Believers should not brag about their spiritual roles or think less of them compared to others. God, who created the body, has placed each part exactly where he wants it ({{1 Corinthians 12:18|12:18}}).
The weaker and less noticeable body parts are very important. They need special care and respect for the whole body to work well.
The church is a united group, so members must live in harmony and care for one another.

- Apostles are special messengers of Christ in the world (see also {{Ephesians 4:11|Ephesians 4:11}}). 

- Prophets deliver messages from God (see {{1 Corinthians 12:10|1 Corinthians 12:10}} and related study note; {{Ephesians 4:11|Ephesians 4:11}}; compare {{Acts 13:1-2|Acts 13:1–2}}). 

- Teachers educate others about the faith ({{Romans 12:7|Romans 12:7}}; {{Ephesians 4:11|Ephesians 4:11}}; compare {{Acts 13:1|Acts 13:1}}). 

- *various tongues:* See study note on 1 Corinthians 12:10.

Paul describes various roles assigned to individuals in the church (see also the list in {{1 Corinthians 12:8-10|12:8–10}}; compare {{Romans 12:6-8|Romans 12:6–8}}; {{Ephesians 4:11|Ephesians 4:11}}).

These rhetorical questions all expect the answer, "Of course not!" Paul gently corrects those who feel jealous of others. Believers should gratefully accept the gifts God has given them. They should not envy other gifts or consider any gifts more important than others (but see {{1 Corinthians 12:31|12:31}}).

- Believers should eagerly seek the most helpful gifts, those with the greatest potential to strengthen the church (see {{1 Corinthians 14:12|14:12}}). They should remember that God distributes gifts as he chooses ({{1 Corinthians 12:11|12:11}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:18|18}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:28|28}}). Paul encourages the Corinthians to look beyond their desire for the gift of tongues (compare {{1 Corinthians 14:1-25|14:1–25}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:27|27}}; see {{1 Corinthians 12:10|12:10}}) because it has the least potential to strengthen the church. 

- *And now I will show you the most excellent way:* This statement leads to Paul’s description of love in {{1 Corinthians 13:1-13|13:1–13}}. Love is the best way of life.

*tongues of men and of angels*: The Corinthians valued the spiritual gift of tongues the most (see also {{1 Corinthians 12:10|12:10}}, {{1 Corinthians 12:28|28}}; {{1 Corinthians 14:1-25|14:1–25}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:27|27}}). Some believed tongues were the language of angels. In Acts, Luke uses the same term for natural human languages (see {{Acts 2:4-13|Acts 2:4–13}}).
Spiritual gifts do not determine our worth to God or the church. Without love, spiritual gifts have no value.

The gifts and abilities that the Spirit gives believers must be used with love. Love isn’t a spiritual gift. Love is a way of living. It’s the way that Jesus taught his followers to live. Paul called it the law of Christ.

He mentioned several ways that people don’t show love. These ways include wanting what belongs to others and bragging. They include people being full of pride and taking care of themselves before others. The Corinthian believers were doing all these things.

Then Paul described the ways of thinking, feeling and acting that are based on love. Love lasts for ever. Spiritual gifts will not last for ever. They are part of the world people live in now that isn’t yet complete. Paul talked about a time when what is complete will come. He was talking about the new creation.

There is a big difference between the world now and the new creation. It’s the difference between looking through a mirror that isn’t clear and looking straight at something. Believers wait with faith and hope for the new creation. As they wait, they follow Jesus’ way of love.

Paul pauses his discussion of spiritual gifts (which he continues in chapter {{1 Corinthians 14:1-40|14}}) to stress that love is more important than any spiritual gift (see {{1 Corinthians 8:1-3|8:1–3}}). The most important goal for Christians is to become deeply and consistently loving individuals.
*If I … can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge*: might refer to the gift of "special knowledge" ({{1 Corinthians 12:8|12:8}}).

- *exult in the surrender of my body*: Some manuscripts say *sacrificed my body to be burned.* A copyist could have easily changed the text by accident, as in Greek, the two readings differ by only one letter. It is unclear which reading is better. However, the manuscripts supporting the reading *exult in* instead of *sacrificed *are generally more reliable. 

- *I gain nothing*: Even the most impressive sacrificial acts mean nothing if not motivated by love.

This description of Christian love highlights the readiness to sacrifice personal desires for the benefit of others (see also {{1 Corinthians 8:1-10:33|8:1–10:33}}; {{Romans 5:6-8|Romans 5:6–8}}; {{Romans 15:3|15:3}}; {{2 Corinthians 8:9|2 Corinthians 8:9}}; {{Philippians 2:4-8|Philippians 2:4–8}}).
*it is not self-seeking*: Love is not self-centered and does not focus only on its own interests (see {{Philippians 2:4-8|Philippians 2:4–8}}).
Love will last forever, because God is love (compare {{1 John 4:7-12|1 John 4:7–12}}, {{1 John 4:16|16}}).
Love, unlike spiritual gifts, will endure forever.
None of the spiritual gifts provides complete understanding. Unlike love, their benefits are limited.

- The difference between now and the future is between this age and the coming age. 

- Now, we see things imperfectly, like puzzling reflections in a mirror. In Paul's time, mirrors were usually made of polished bronze, so the view was unclear. Our perception in this life is limited, and our understanding is incomplete. 

- Then, when the end comes and Christ establishes his eternal kingdom, we will see everything clearly. At that time, the spiritual gifts that provide knowledge will no longer be needed.

Faith, hope, and love are more important than spiritual gifts because they last forever (see also {{Romans 5:1-5|Romans 5:1–5}}; {{Galatians 5:5-6|Galatians 5:5–6}}; {{Colossians 1:4-5|Colossians 1:4–5}}; {{1 Thessalonians 1:3|1 Thessalonians 1:3}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:8|5:8}}). Of the three, the greatest is love, because love is the essential nature of God himself (see {{1 John 4:7-12|1 John 4:7–12}}, {{1 John 4:16-21|16–21}}). Therefore, love should define our relationship with him and others.

Among all the special abilities the Spirit provides (see study note on 1 Corinthians 12:1–14:40), Paul urges the Corinthians to seek the ability to prophesy because it benefits the church more (see {{1 Corinthians 12:10|12:10}}) .

Some believers in Corinth thought that certain spiritual gifts were better than others. Paul made it clear that this wasn’t true. The gifts have different purposes.

Many Corinthian believers could speak other languages. These were languages that they didn’t know before. They were proud of this gift of the Spirit. Paul showed why they should desire the gift of prophecy more than other gifts. He described the gifts based on how much they encourage and help others.

When people speak in languages they didn’t know before, it helps them pray to God. They are strengthened in their relationship with God. That is a wonderful thing. But other people don’t understand what they are saying. They can only understand if there is someone who can explain other languages. If the message isn’t explained, those listening to it aren’t strengthened or encouraged. And they may become confused.

It’s much more helpful for believers to share prophecies in a language everyone understands. This can help others recognise sinful ways in their lives. It can also comfort them and give them hope. The important thing is for believers to use their gifts in ways that strengthen the church.

After highlighting the supreme importance of love (chapter {{1 Corinthians 13:1-13|13}}), Paul discusses spiritual gifts again. He defines their value by how much they help others, which reflects love (chapter {{1 Corinthians 13:1-13|13}}). With this in mind, Paul compares the overvalued gift of speaking in tongues with the more helpful gift of prophecy.

The issue with speaking in tongues is that listeners cannot easily understand the message. However, the gift of prophecy is clear and helpful. It is a message from God that strengthens, encourages, and comforts those who hear it.
The main purpose of spiritual gifts is to strengthen the whole church, not just to improve oneself (see {{1 Corinthians 12:7|12:7}}; compare {{1 Corinthians 8:1|8:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 14:12|14:12}}).
A message must be clear to communicate well.
The Spirit gives special abilities to strengthen the entire church (see {{1 Corinthians 12:7|12:7}}; {{1 Corinthians 14:4|14:4}}; compare {{Ephesians 4:15-16|Ephesians 4:15–16}}).
Paul does not forbid speaking in tongues (see {{1 Corinthians 14:39|14:39}}), but interpreting is crucial, especially in public worship (see {{1 Corinthians 14:27-28|14:27–28}}).
Speaking in tongues involves the speaker's spirit, as the Holy Spirit speaks through them, but not their mind, since the message is not logically understandable.

- It is better to worship with both spirit and understandable words. Public worship should bless God and others. Speaking in tongues without interpretation glorifies God and helps the speaker ({{1 Corinthians 14:4|14:4}}), but it does not help others present. 

- *say “Amen” to your thanksgiving: Amen* was the traditional response to a prayer.
Paul emphasized the personal benefit of speaking in tongues, but in a church meeting, it should benefit others, not just the speaker.
To understand these matters maturely, consider the purpose of spiritual gifts. Do not treat them as ends for personal enjoyment.

Paul used this quotation from {{Isaiah 28:11-12|Isaiah 28:11–12}} to show that speaking in tongues is a sign for unbelievers, not believers. However, in {{1 Corinthians 14:23-25|1 Corinthians 14:23–25}}, Paul argues that unbelievers are more likely to be convinced by prophecy than by speaking in tongues. He emphasizes that, in public worship, prophecy is more useful than speaking in tongues.
*“God is truly among you!”* Paul refers to {{Isaiah 45:14|Isaiah 45:14}}.

- *has a psalm: P*salms can be sung alone or with others (compare {{Ephesians 5:19|Ephesians 5:19}}; {{Colossians 3:16|Colossians 3:16}}). 

- Everything done in public worship should strengthen the church (see {{1 Corinthians 12:7|1 Corinthians 12:7}}; {{1 Corinthians 14:4|14:4}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:6|6}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:12|12}}, {{1 Corinthians 14:26|26}}; see also {{1 Corinthians 8:1|8:1}}).

The Corinthian believers used their gifts from the Holy Spirit in their worship services. They were very active and excited as they worshipped God. Paul recognised that this was good.

But there were certain problems when the Corinthians gathered together. Their services were wild and out of control. People were sharing messages in languages that no one understood. It was hard to hear anything because many people were prophesying at the same time. Some women talked too loudly. They kept other believers from paying attention.

So Paul gave the Corinthians instructions to follow in their services. God is a God of peace and order. Believers must use their gifts in ways that show God’s order.

Paul provides clear instructions for using spiritual gifts in the church. He stresses the importance of expressing them in an orderly manner. In the early Christian community, church meetings were not led by professional pastors or priests. Instead, everyone shared what God had given them to strengthen the church.
Paul advises a church eager for the gift of tongues to limit its public use. He suggests no more than two or three people should speak, one at a time, and only if someone can interpret the message.

Public prophecy should be shared in an orderly manner, guided by the Spirit, so everyone benefits. Others should evaluate what is said to determine if it is truly a message from God ({{1 Thessalonians 5:19-21|1 Thessalonians 5:19–21}}). Those with a prophecy should take turns. Although prophecy is a divinely given message, the speaker still controls it.

- This part of the discussion on using spiritual gifts shows a view on women's roles similar to that of the Pastoral Letters (see {{1 Timothy 2:11-15|1 Timothy 2:11–15}}). 

- Paul advises women to be quiet and respectful in church meetings. We should understand this instruction considering {{1 Corinthians 11:5|1 Corinthians 11:5}}, which clearly implies that women can pray and prophesy in public. 

- *as the law says*: This possibly refers to {{Genesis 3:16|Genesis 3:16}}.

- As an apostle, Paul wanted the Corinthians to treat his words as commands from the Lord. 

- *What I am writing you*: This likely refers to all his teachings, especially about spiritual gifts.
Paul summarizes his discussion on spiritual gifts in chapters {{1 Corinthians 12:1-14:40|12 to 14}}.
The main message of the good news is the message of Christ's sacrificial death and resurrection (see {{1 Corinthians 15:3-4|15:3–4}}; {{Romans 5:8-10|Romans 5:8–10}}; {{Romans 6:5-11|6:5–11}}).
Paul summarizes the good news about Jesus he preached.

Jesus Christ is the Messiah who died and then was raised from the dead. This is at the very centre of the good news about Jesus.

Paul preached this message to the Corinthians. It was the message that all of Jesus’ apostles preached. The apostles and many others had seen Jesus after he was raised from the dead. They were witnesses to his resurrection.

But some believers in Corinth were saying that this message wasn’t true. They didn’t believe that anyone could be raised from the dead. Paul strongly opposed this way of thinking. If no one can be raised from the dead, then Christ himself wasn’t raised. Without his resurrection, there is no good news about Jesus.

The good news is about God’s victory over sin and death. Jesus’ resurrection from the dead is the sign that God’s victory is real. Without it, believers can’t hope for life after they die. Without Jesus’ resurrection, faith in Jesus has no meaning.
Some church members doubted a future resurrection of the dead. Paul reassures them and addresses their skeptical questions by discussing the nature of a resurrection body.

*If you hold firmly to the word I preached to you*: Those who stay strong in their faith will find salvation (see {{Matthew 10:22|Matthew 10:22}}; {{Matthew 24:13|24:13}}; {{John 15:6|John 15:6}}; {{Galatians 5:4|Galatians 5:4}}; {{Colossians 1:23|Colossians 1:23}}; {{Hebrews 6:4-6|Hebrews 6:4–6}}; contrast with {{1 Corinthians 1:8|1 Corinthians 1:8}}; {{Romans 8:38-39|Romans 8:38–39}}; {{Philippians 1:6|Philippians 1:6}}; {{Hebrews 6:9|Hebrews 6:9}}).

The main message of the good news is that Christ died for our sins (see {{Romans 3:24-25|Romans 3:24–25}}; {{Romans 5:8-10|5:8–10}}; {{Galatians 1:4|Galatians 1:4}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:9-10|1 Thessalonians 5:9–10}}).

- *He appeared to Cephas*: See {{Luke 24:34|Luke 24:34}}. 

- *then to the Twelve*: See {{Matthew 28:16-17|Matthew 28:16–17}}; {{Mark 16:14|Mark 16:14}}; {{Luke 24:36|Luke 24:36}}; {{John 20:19|John 20:19}}.

More than 500 people saw him. We have no other record of this event. Most of these witnesses were still alive when this letter was written (around AD 53–56). People could verify Christ’s resurrection by asking these living eyewitnesses.

*Then He appeared to James*: This James was almost certainly the brother of Jesus. He became a leader of the Jerusalem church after Jesus died (see {{Mark 6:3|Mark 6:3}}; {{John 7:1-5|John 7:1–5}}; {{Galatians 1:19|Galatians 1:19}}; compare {{Acts 12:17|Acts 12:17}}; {{Acts 15:13|15:13}}; {{Acts 21:18|21:18}}).

- *as to one of untimely birth*: This phrase can refer to a miscarriage or stillbirth. Here it might describe the unusual way Paul converted, the negative view some opponents had of his role as an apostle, or his own feelings of unworthiness to be an apostle. The main focus is on God's extraordinary grace to Paul, who once persecuted Christ’s followers (see {{Galatians 1:13|Galatians 1:13}}; {{Philippians 3:6|Philippians 3:6}}; compare {{Acts 8:3|Acts 8:3}}; {{Acts 9:1-2|9:1–2}}). 

- *He appeared to me also*: Paul met the risen Christ during his conversion (see {{1 Corinthians 9:1|1 Corinthians 9:1}}; {{Acts 9:3-6|Acts 9:3–6}}; {{Galatians 1:15-16|Galatians 1:15–16}}).

*But by the grace of God*: Paul understood God's special favor, or *grace*, towards him, which led to an extraordinary response. This response was also God working through Paul by his grace (see {{2 Corinthians 4:7|2 Corinthians 4:7}}; {{Galatians 2:20|Galatians 2:20}}; {{Colossians 1:27|Colossians 1:27}}).
The important thing is the message, not the people delivering it (compare{{1 Corinthians 1:10-12|1:10–12}}).
Some believers in Corinth struggled to accept the Jewish idea of a bodily resurrection. They preferred the Greek idea of the soul's immortality (compare {{Acts 17:18|Acts 17:18}}, {{Acts 17:32|32}}).
The resurrection of Jesus proves that a future resurrection is real.
Paul argues for a future resurrection.

If Christ did not rise from the dead, then the Christian faith is pointless. However, Jesus’ resurrection proves that His sacrifice completely atoned for human sins (see {{1 Corinthians 15:3|15:3}}). Without Christ's resurrection, people remain unforgiven and under God's judgment, still guilty of their sins (see {{Romans 3:19|Romans 3:19}}; {{Ephesians 2:1-3|Ephesians 2:1–3}}).

Without eternal life, faithful believers deserve pity more than anyone else because they face persecution and hardship. However, they find joy in looking forward to what comes after this life, just like Jesus (see {{Hebrews 12:2|Hebrews 12:2}}) and Paul (see {{2 Corinthians 4:16-18|2 Corinthians 4:16–18}}; {{Philippians 1:21-23|Philippians 1:21–23}}; {{Philippians 3:7-11|3:7–11}}).

In the Old Testament, people dedicated the first crop to God (see {{Exodus 23:19|Exodus 23:19}}). Christ’s resurrection is the first of many resurrections of God’s people (see {{Colossians 1:18|Colossians 1:18}}).

Paul talked about what Adam did. He was talking about Adam’s sin. When Adam sinned, sin and death entered the world. The result is that human beings die.

Paul also talked about what Christ did. He was talking about how Jesus lived without sinning. Jesus died like Adam did and like all humans do. But then God raised him from the dead. Jesus was the first human to have new powerful eternal life from God. He shares that life with all who follow him. They will all be raised from the dead when Jesus returns to earth. At that time he will destroy evil, sin and death completely.

This is the hope that Paul shared with all the churches he helped start. This hope gave him strength to face troubles and suffering. It also helps believers to face the troubles and suffering in their lives.
Adam's sin contrasts with Christ's resurrection (compare {{1 Corinthians 15:45-49|15:45–49}}).

*dominion, authority, and power*: This phrase refers to spiritual forces that oppose Christ (compare {{Romans 8:38|Romans 8:38}}; {{Ephesians 1:21|Ephesians 1:21}}; {{Colossians 2:10|Colossians 2:10}}, {{Colossians 2:15|15}}; {{1 Peter 3:22|1 Peter 3:22}}).
Christ is the Lord of everything, including death. However, he is still under the authority of God, his Father.

- This paraphrase of {{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}} refers to Jesus (compare {{Hebrews 1:13|Hebrews 1:13}}). 

- *God has put everything under His feet*: In the ancient Near East, artists showed victorious kings with their feet on the necks of their defeated enemies.
*everything has been put under Him*: See {{Psalm 8:6|Psalm 8:6}}; compare {{Matthew 22:44|Matthew 22:44}}.

Some first-century Christians practiced baptism by proxy for dead unbelievers they wanted to save. Paul does not endorse or condemn this practice; he uses it as evidence for belief in resurrection. Early Christian literature does not mention this practice elsewhere.
The apostles risked their lives because they believed in life after death. Without resurrection, their suffering would be meaningless.

*If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus*: Paul uses this phrase to describe his struggles with opponents in Ephesus (see {{1 Corinthians 16:8|16:8}}; {{Acts 19:23-41|Acts 19:23–41}}; {{2 Corinthians 1:8|2 Corinthians 1:8}}; {{2 Corinthians 4:8-12|4:8–12}}; {{2 Corinthians 11:23-28|11:23–28}}). Watching condemned prisoners fight wild beasts and get mauled to death was common entertainment in the Roman world.
*"Bad company corrupts good character"*: This quote comes from the Greek poet Menander, who lived in the 300s BC. Paul uses it as a warning not to follow or listen to people who teach what is false.
*some of you are ignorant of God*: Paul strongly criticizes those who are proud of their knowledge but doubt the resurrection.

Paul taught that the bodies of all believers will be raised from the dead. Some of the Corinthian believers couldn’t understand what their bodies would be like when this happened. Paul used things they could see on earth as examples to help them understand.

A plant looks very different from the seed it grew from. This is the same as the difference between a person’s body before death and after resurrection. Human bodies are made of things God created when he made the world. In this way they are like the body God created from the dust for Adam (Genesis 2:7). That is what Paul meant about being like the earthly man.

When believers are raised from the dead, their human bodies will be changed. They will not be only a spirit. They will have bodies like Jesus’ body after he rose from the dead. That is what Paul meant about being like the heavenly man. Their new bodies will be able to do much more than their old bodies. Their new bodies will last for ever.

Paul celebrates this with a victory song. The Messiah lives and death’s power has been taken away! The way that people live while they are on earth is important. It’s important because death isn’t the end of life.
Paul talks about what resurrection bodies are like, possibly answering doubts. In the Greco-Roman world, people often believed the soul was immortal, but not that the body could rise again.
*You fool!*: Paul’s strong response suggests skepticism. It might also imply that the answer cannot be known.

Just as a plant's shape does not look like its seed, the seed still determines the plant's growth. Similarly, the resurrection body will differ from the current body but will still be recognizable as the same person.
Everything God has made has its own glory. This means each thing has its own beauty and greatness. The resurrection body will also be different. It will not be like anything else.
Resurrection bodies will be very different from our mortal bodies, just as plants differ from the seeds they grow from.
Just as Christ's life-giving Spirit goes beyond natural life, the spiritual body will replace the physical body.

Adam and Christ created two different groups of people. One group is natural and earthly, bound by sin and death. The other group is spiritual and heavenly, cleansed and meant for life. Adam symbolizes the natural, physical body, while Christ represents the spiritual, resurrected body. See also {{1 Corinthians 15:21-22|15:21–22}}; {{Romans 5:12-21|Romans 5:12–21}}.
Adam was made from the dust of the earth ({{Genesis 2:7|Genesis 2:7}}), showing his earthly origin. This contrasts with Christ's heavenly origin.

- *Earthly man*: Like Adam, natural human beings face the curse of sin and death. All return to dust (see {{Genesis 3:19|Genesis 3:19}}). They all die. 

- *as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are of heaven*: Those who belong to Christ share in his eternal spiritual life.

Like Adam, the first man, we have physical bodies in this life. But one day, we will be like Christ, the heavenly man, and experience the kingdom of God with resurrection bodies (compare {{Romans 6:4-14|Romans 6:4–14}}).
Physical bodies cannot enter God's kingdom. Only a spiritual, resurrected body can fully experience the kingdom (compare {{John 4:24|John 4:24}}).

- The good news about Jesus reveals the once unknown secret of resurrection. 

- *We will not all sleep*: Paul might have expected the future resurrection during his own lifetime (compare {{1 Corinthians 15:52|15:52}}; {{1 Thessalonians 4:15|1 Thessalonians 4:15}}, {{1 Thessalonians 4:17|17}}).

*"Death has been swallowed up in victory"*: Resurrection defeats the ultimate enemy, death. The power of the Spirit helps believers overcome sin now (see {{Romans 8:2|Romans 8:2}}, {{Romans 8:11|11}}).

- This quote from ({{Hosea 13:14|Hosea 13:14}} assures believers they need not fear death. 

- Death is compared to the sting of a scorpion.
The death and resurrection of Christ end the control of sin and death (see {{Romans 6:14|Romans 6:14}}; {{Romans 8:2|8:2}}; {{Romans 10:4|10:4}}).
*your labor in the Lord is not in vain*: Those who serve him faithfully will receive eternal rewards (see {{1 Corinthians 3:12-15|3:12–15}}).
Galatia was a Roman province in Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey (see {{Acts 16:6|Acts 16:6}}; {{Acts 18:23|18:23}}).

Paul responds to the Corinthians' question about the donation for poor Christians in Jerusalem ({{Acts 24:17|Acts 24:17}}; {{Romans 15:25-27|Romans 15:25–27}}; {{2 Corinthians 8:1-9:15|Second Corinthians 8–9}}; {{Galatians 2:10|Galatians 2:10}}).

The Corinthian believers joined other Gentile churches in preparing an offering of money. It was for Jewish believers in Jerusalem who were needy.

Paul gave them instructions about preparing their gift in a proper and orderly way. Paul also wrote about this offering in Romans 15:25–28 and in 2 Corinthians 8–9. He hoped to visit the Corinthian church to collect the offering.

Paul mentioned several friends that he and the Corinthian believers knew. These friends were examples of people who work hard, give freely and serve others. Paul wanted the Corinthians to treat them well and to follow their example.

Paul closed his letter with commands about being prepared, being brave and being loving. This included telling the believers to greet each other with a holy kiss. This practice showed that believers accepted one another as family members. It also showed that they treated one another with respect and honour. It was a way to show their love for the Lord and all his people.

Christians gathered on the first day of each week (see {{Acts 20:7|Acts 20:7}}) instead of the last day, as in the Old Testament ({{Exodus 20:8|Exodus 20:8}}; {{Exodus 34:21|34:21}}; {{Isaiah 58:13-14|Isaiah 58:13–14}}). The first day was called the "Lord's Day," marking the day of the Lord's resurrection ({{Mark 16:9|Mark 16:9}}; {{Luke 24:13-15|Luke 24:13–15}}; {{John 20:19|John 20:19}}; {{Revelation 1:10|Revelation 1:10}}). The amount of money to give was not specified. Paul later encouraged them to give as generously as possible ({{2 Corinthians 8:1-4|2 Corinthians 8:1–4}}; {{2 Corinthians 9:6-13|9:6–13}}; compare {{Luke 12:33-34|Luke 12:33–34}}; {{Luke 21:1-4|21:1–4}}; {{1 Timothy 6:18-19|1 Timothy 6:18–19}}).
Paul delivered the gift to Jerusalem ({{Romans 15:25-26|Romans 15:25–26}}).

- Paul traveled through Macedonia, a Roman province in northern Greece, during his second missionary journey ({{Acts 15:36-18:22|Acts 15:36–18:22}}). 

- He planned to travel through Macedonia again (See {{Acts 19:21|Acts 19:21}}; {{Acts 20:1-3|20:1–3}}).
*or even spend the winter*: Paul evidently did visit during the winter (compare {{Acts 20:2-3|Acts 20:2–3}}).

- Paul wrote this letter while he was in Ephesus, around AD 53 to 56 ({{Acts 19:1-20|Acts 19:1–20:1}}). 

- Pentecost occurred in May or June.

- *If Timothy comes*: See {{1 Corinthians 4:17|4:17}}. Timothy was Paul's spiritual child and co-worker (see {{1 Timothy 1:2|1 Timothy 1:2}}). 

- *see to it that he has nothing to fear*: Timothy might have been shy or tentative ({{2 Timothy 1:6-8|2 Timothy 1:6–8}}).
*our brother Apollos*: Refer to study note on 1 Corinthians 1:12.
Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus traveled from Corinth to visit Paul in Ephesus (see also {{1 Corinthians 1:16|1:16}}; {{1 Corinthians 16:15|16:15}}).

- Aquila and Priscilla (also called Prisca in Greek) had moved from Corinth to Ephesus, where Paul wrote this letter (compare {{Acts 18:1-3|Acts 18:1–3}}). 

- *the church that meets at their house*: Aquila and Priscilla later continued this practice in Rome (see {{Romans 16:3-5|Romans 16:3–5}}).
Like in his other letters, Paul greets his friends and offers a blessing.
*Greet one another with a holy kiss*: People often greeted each other with a kiss on the cheek.

Paul ends the letter by writing a few words in his own handwriting. In those times, it was common for someone else to write down the letter as a secretary. Paul did this in this letter and in others (see {{Romans 16:22|Romans 16:22}}; {{Galatians 6:11|Galatians 6:11}}; {{Colossians 4:18|Colossians 4:18}}; {{2 Thessalonians 3:17|2 Thessalonians 3:17}}).

- To be cursed means to be condemned by God (see also {{Romans 9:3|Romans 9:3}}; {{Galatians 1:8-9|Galatians 1:8–9}}). 

- *Come, O Lord!*: Early Christians sometimes used this phrase in prayers (see also {{Revelation 22:20|Revelation 22:20}}).

- All of Paul's letters end with a blessing like this one. 

- Paul mentions grace at both the start and end of this letter (see {{1 Corinthians 1:3|1:3}}).
